content_metadata.description: A video segment featuring news anchor Katy and journalist Mona Eltahawy discussing women's role in the Arab Spring and the ongoing fight for women's rights in the Middle East.

qAndA.answer: Mona is wearing a large, multi-layered silver necklace with a central round pendant and several smaller round pendants.
qAndA.question: What type of necklace is Mona wearing?

qAndA.answer: Mona argues that women's rights are still in jeopardy despite the Arab Spring, as they face deep-seated patriarchal attitudes and oppression in the region. She believes a 'gender revolution' is necessary to achieve true freedom and dignity for women.
qAndA.question: What is the main argument presented in Mona's essay?

qAndA.answer: Mona recounts the incident where six or seven soldiers violently stomped on a woman in Tahrir Square in December, highlighting the intense level of misogyny and aggression women experience.
qAndA.question: What example does Mona provide to illustrate the 'hate' she describes?

qAndA.answer: Mona speaks with passion and conviction, using emphatic gestures to emphasize her points. This reinforces the mood of determination and underscores the urgency of the issue she is discussing.
qAndA.question: How does Mona's tone and body language contribute to the mood of the interview?

qAndA.answer: The background likely represents Mona's current location but also visually contrasts the more liberal and progressive environment of the West with the oppressive conditions she describes in the Middle East, further highlighting the urgency of the problem.
qAndA.question: What is the symbolic significance of Mona's New York City background during the interview?

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: From Libya to Egypt to Syria, as we have watched revolutions unfold, we have seen women spurring change.
They've been there right at the front of the demonstrations, risking their lives for new leaders
and new rights. So perhaps no one has more riding on the outcome of the Arab Spring than the women
who have lived under oppression and now hope for freedom. But will they get it?
In the new cover article for Foreign Policy magazine, Egyptian American journalist Mona El-Tawahi
asks, why do they hate us? She warns that the rights of women in the Arab world are
a little insurious jeopardy. Mona joins me now from New York. Mona, thank you very much for joining me
with this very powerful article. First of all, explain the role women have played in the course of the
Arab Spring. Women have been on the front lines of every single uprising in revolution that we
witnessed in the region since Muhammad Boazizi set himself on fire in Tunisia of December of 2010,
whether it's in Syria today where we still see that incredible courage alongside men
or in Egypt where inside jails, outside of jails or in Tunisia, where they're building their
country towards a new constitution. Women have been front and center alongside men, which is why
it's really important that we think of the second revolution, the revolution that will continue
this one, which I believe must be a gender revolution. Okay, Mona, what was it that those women
who are in the front lines of these revolutions were asking for? What did they want from change?
Well, they wanted freedom and dignity, which have been the catch words or the themes of all the
revolutions across the region. Now, in Egypt, for example, Hosni Mubarak oppressed all of Egypt,
but when we take Hosni Mubarak outside of the picture, the Selamul Barak in our minds,
there's a Mubarak in our bedrooms, there's a Mubarak in the streets, because Egyptian society,
in its conservative patriarchal attitudes towards women, oppresses Egyptian women. So it's like a
hierarchy of oppression. So when women went out on the street, they were fighting the patriarch,
Mubarak. But many of the women I know there on the street, and when I go back and demonstrate
with them, we're now fighting against the small patriarchs, which is that conservative attitude
that does not believe in freedom and dignity for all. Okay, and in terms of the governments that
have taken over in places like Tunisia and in Libya and we're still waiting in Egypt, have they
given women the things that they were asking for from the revolution? Have they paid them back
effectively? Well, at least in Tunisia, they have more than 40 women in their constituent assembly,
and that speaks to the high visibility of Tunisian women in their country. But in my country,
birth Egypt, in our constituent assembly, which has now been disbanded, thankfully, or suspended,
out of 100 members, only seven were women, and that is a shameful and disgraceful number.
So the point of my essay is that the revolutions in the Middle Eastern or South Africa were
started by a man, Muhammad Boazizi, and they will be complicit by women, because it's women who
understand the freedom and dignity that truly lie at the heart of these uprisings. Okay, but Mona,
you also, I mean, you have this very provocative title, Why Do They Hate Us? And your suggestion is
that women are not going to get the kind of dignity and freedom and equality that they want in
the Middle East because they are, as you put it, hated by their men folk. Right, one of the
points I make is that we don't have any freedoms in the Middle Eastern or South Africa because they hate
us. And that's why I'm saying that what's going on in on the ground there now, be it through various
feminist movements or individual activists who stood up to the military junta in Egypt or others,
what they're doing is they're saying we demand those rights, just as the populations that
rose up said we demand freedom and dignity. Women are saying we demand it because we can't wait
until it's given to us. We have to fight for it. Briefly, Mona, you do think hatred is the
right word? Is that what you feel women suffer in the Middle East? I do, Katty, because a picture
that illustrates my essay is of the six or seven soldiers that were stomping very violently on a
woman in Tahliu Square in December. And that level of viciousness is truly hatred. And I know it's
a provocative word and I think we need to be provocative. We need to poke. And so as a writer,
I think it's my job, it's my role to poke the painful places. And so I use hate to be controversial
and to make people really ask what's going on. Okay, Mona El-Tawahi is a very strong piece. Thank
you so much for joining me, Mona. Thanks.

youtube_description:
(BBC) Help
In a striking cover article for Foreign Policy magazine, Egyptian-American writer Mona Eltahawy argues that women must finish the revolutions started by the Arab Spring.

Eltahawy tells the BBC's Katty Kay that post-Mubarak Egypt has not provided women with the basic freedoms that all Egyptians asked for during the revolution.

"Just as the populations who rose up demanding freedom and dignity, women are saying we demand it," Eltahawy said. "Because we can't wait until it's given to us."
youtube_title: Mona Eltahawy: 'Why Do They Hate Us?'
